correctness.rationale: The first three coefficients of log 0F1(;a;s/2) give the stated Bessel cumulants under generator (1/2)Δ. In Gamma-minus-Bessel order, the standardized third cumulant difference divided by six is −a/[3(a+2)√(a+1)]. For the Bessel product, the lower bound on the inverse-square potential bounds every standardized exponential weight by O(a^−1/2); the Dirichlet test functions on [1/2,1] bound the first floor(a) weights below by a constant times a^−1/2. Their squares sum to one, so fourth powers sum to O(a^−1). The expansion on |u|≤a^(1/16) has integrated remainder O(a^−1) against du/|u|, by the Gaussian times the fourth- and sixth-power bounds. On a^(1/16)≤|u|≤a the squared weights and log(1+x)≥x/(1+x) yield a stretched-exponential bound; beyond a, the floor(a) lower-bounded weights give an integrable power tail. The Gamma characteristic function has the corresponding bounds directly from its shape. Signed inversion is legitimate since the difference divided by u is integrable. Integrating H3φ yields −H2φ, so the sign in the Finding is correct, including a negative Gamma-minus-Bessel CDF difference at the mean to leading order. The off-center absolute extrema have relative height 2e^(−3/2)<1; taking the uniform supremum proves the constant. The Bessel formulation is valid for real a, and the Brownian formulation applies when 2a is integral. Verification evidence is finite and was inspected, not used as an asymptotic proof or executed.
residual_risks: No optimized numerical constant for the asymptotic remainder or relative-tail control is established.

value.rationale: The large-index regime is a natural stress test of the existing simplest moment-optimal approximant. The signed profile tells where and in which direction that approximant errs, while the nonzero constant quantifies a leading-order obstruction that moment matching or a central limit theorem alone would miss. The uniform remainder justifies optimization over thresholds.
residual_risks: Value is for absolute CDF error on this centered exit problem, not relative rare-event accuracy or joint limits in approximation order and dimension.
